title: Multilingual retrieval without losing names, units or permissions
summary: Search across languages while preserving exact entities and measuring answer support in the language of the source.
body:
Search across languages while preserving exact entities and measuring answer support in the language of the source.

Treat language as a retrieval constraint

Multilingual retrieval finds evidence when the question and the answer-bearing document use different languages or scripts. A Hindi request for a pump's pressure limit might need an English maintenance sheet. Translate or encode the request for candidate generation, but retain the original request and its entity spans. A translated product name can become a common noun; a model number or unit can be silently changed. Keep the original tokens beside any expansion so the exact identifier remains searchable. Expansion tests should fail when an alias changes the requested entity.

Use two candidate paths

A multilingual vector index can find semantically related passages across languages; an exact or transliterated term index can recover names and part numbers that an embedding misses. Merge bounded candidate lists, then rank the original passages. Transliteration is a controlled alias for a named entity, not a general translation engine. Store aliases with locale, entity ID and review status. If two entities share the same Roman spelling, an alias must not erase that ambiguity. Hybrid merging gives a practical way to combine the two paths without pretending their raw scores are comparable.

Preserve the source's meaning

Retrieve source text, revision, locale and passage ID together. A translated display excerpt may help the reader, but the citation must still point to the original passage. Numbers, negation, effective dates and units require explicit checks across the translation boundary. Do not answer a question in the user's language from a passage whose translation has inverted 'must not' or converted 47 psi into 47 kPa. Claim-level support is judged against the source, not against a fluent paraphrase.

Filter before mixing languages

Tenant permissions, document status and jurisdiction apply to every language variant. A public English summary is not evidence that a private Spanish appendix can be searched or surfaced. Deduplicate translations by source lineage only after access filtering; separate independently authored statements even if they are translated similarly. Track source revision across language copies because a translated page may lag behind the original. Corpus lifecycle determines which variant is eligible.

Evaluate language pairs, not one average

Build judged queries for each query-language and document-language pair, including mixed-script queries, transliterated names, similar identifiers and documents with no valid answer. Report candidate recall, supported answer rate and entity preservation per pair. A strong English-English score can hide total failure on Hindi-English or Arabic-English searches. Review wrong answers with both original and translated passages. If no reviewer can establish the meaning of the source, mark support unknown rather than accepting the answer by fluency.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass
import unicodedata

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ServicePassage:
    passage_id: str
    tenant: str
    locale: str
    text: str
    entity_id: str

def normalized(text: str) -> str:
    return unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text).casefold()

def exact_entity_candidates(passages: list[ServicePassage], tenant: str,
                            requested_entity: str, aliases: dict[str, str]) -> list[str]:
    entity_id = aliases.get(normalized(requested_entity))
    if entity_id is None:
        return []
    return [passage.passage_id for passage in passages
            if passage.tenant == tenant and passage.entity_id == entity_id]

service_notes = [ServicePassage("sheet-en-r4", "north", "en",
                                "Pump P-47 relief limit is 83 kPa.", "pump-p47"),
                 ServicePassage("sheet-hi-r2", "south", "hi",
                                "P-47 limit is 99 kPa.", "pump-p47")]
reviewed_aliases = {normalized("पी-47"): "pump-p47", normalized("P-47"): "pump-p47"}
assert exact_entity_candidates(service_notes, "north", "पी-47", reviewed_aliases) == ["sheet-en-r4"]
assert exact_entity_candidates(service_notes, "north", "P-48", reviewed_aliases) == []

Performance and operating cost

The transparent candidate scan costs O(N) time over N passages and O(K) output space for K eligible matches. A production entity index keyed by tenant and entity ID reduces lookup work but requires reviewed aliases and refreshes when documents change. A second multilingual vector path adds index storage and query latency; measure its incremental supported recall by language pair before accepting the cost.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating transliteration as an unambiguous entity identifier.
  • Dropping the original query after translation and losing exact numbers or negation.
  • Citing only a generated translation rather than the source passage.
  • Reporting one aggregate recall score across uneven language pairs.

Validation drill

Build 53 questions across three query languages and two document languages. Include twelve mixed-script identifiers and eight restricted passages. Record entity preservation, authorized candidate recall and supported answers for every language pair.

title: Code repository retrieval by symbol, call site and commit
summary: Find implementation evidence in a changing repository without confusing symbol matches, generated files and stale revisions.
body:
Find implementation evidence in a changing repository without confusing symbol matches, generated files and stale revisions.

Index code as code

Code repository retrieval searches declarations, call sites, configuration and tests as related but distinct evidence. A question about how InvoiceLedger.post records a refund needs the method body and perhaps its caller; a README mentioning the same method is insufficient. Parse source into language-aware symbols with file path, line span and commit ID. Preserve surrounding imports and enclosing class for interpretation. Stable chunk identity helps trace a symbol across index rebuilds, but a changed body must receive a new revision identity.

Use the repository graph carefully

Exact symbol search should usually run before semantic search for named functions, exception types or environment keys. Then collect bounded callers, callees and tests to explain behavior. A call graph is only an approximation in languages with reflection, runtime dispatch, generated code or dependency injection. Do not claim a path is unreachable because a static extractor missed it. Edge provenance should identify whether an edge came from parsing, a build artifact or a test trace.

Bind every result to a revision

Branch names move. A result retrieved from main yesterday may contradict today's implementation. Store commit, file hash and language in the index; include the commit in the answer trace. For a question about a deployment, use the deployed commit rather than the latest default branch. For a historical bug, retrieve the failing revision and a candidate fix separately. Temporal evidence is particularly important when a config flag changed between releases.

Respect boundaries and noise

Filter repositories and paths by permission before presenting symbol names or snippets. Skip vendored libraries, generated files and copied lockfile text unless the question specifically concerns them. Merge duplicate definitions only when lineage and revision match. Keep tests accessible as evidence of intended behavior, but do not treat a passing test as proof that every production call follows the same path. Duplicate handling should not collapse a test and implementation into one source.

Judge answer-bearing spans

Create questions about exact symbols, renamed methods, inherited calls, generated bindings, stale commits and behavior described only by a caller. Measure whether the correct file and line span entered the candidate set, whether the required call path was retrieved, and whether the final explanation cited the right revision. A high lexical hit on a symbol name is not a supported answer if its body never entered context. Keep line links pinned to commit hashes so they remain valid after later edits.

Worked contract

import ast
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CodeSymbol:
    name: str
    path: str
    commit: str
    first_line: int
    last_line: int

def python_symbols(source: str, path: str, commit: str) -> list[CodeSymbol]:
    tree = ast.parse(source, filename=path)
    symbols: list[CodeSymbol] = []
    for node in tree.body:
        if isinstance(node, (ast.FunctionDef, ast.AsyncFunctionDef)):
            symbols.append(CodeSymbol(node.name, path, commit, node.lineno, node.end_lineno))
        elif isinstance(node, ast.ClassDef):
            for method in node.body:
                if isinstance(method, (ast.FunctionDef, ast.AsyncFunctionDef)):
                    symbols.append(CodeSymbol(f"{node.name}.{method.name}", path,
                                              commit, method.lineno, method.end_lineno))
    return symbols

ledger_source = "class InvoiceLedger:\n    def post_refund(self, amount):\n        return -amount\n"
found = python_symbols(ledger_source, "billing/ledger.py", "c47e2a")
assert found == [CodeSymbol("InvoiceLedger.post_refund", "billing/ledger.py", "c47e2a", 2, 3)]

Performance and operating cost

AST extraction visits O(S) syntax nodes and stores O(M) symbols for M declarations. An exact symbol index is cheap to query but misses indirect behavior; graph expansion can grow rapidly with call depth, so cap neighbors and inspect the highest-value paths first. Parsing each changed file once per commit is cheaper than rescanning the full repository on every question.

Common Mistakes

  • Answering from a README when the question asks what code actually executes.
  • Mixing snippets from different commits in one behavior claim.
  • Assuming a static call graph captures reflective or injected calls.
  • Indexing vendored and generated code as if it were the repository's own implementation.

Validation drill

Index 47 source files at two commits. Judge 41 questions about named methods, indirect callers and renamed symbols; report correct commit, symbol span and supported call-path coverage separately.

title: Audio and video retrieval with timecoded evidence
summary: Retrieve a precise spoken or visual moment while retaining timestamps, speakers and media-version identity.
body:
Retrieve a precise spoken or visual moment while retaining timestamps, speakers and media-version identity.

Make time part of the passage ID

Audio and video retrieval uses timed segments, transcript words and sometimes frame descriptions as searchable evidence. A transcript paragraph without a start and end time cannot support a jump to the original recording. Store media asset ID, version, track, speaker label, start and end milliseconds on every segment. Re-captioning or editing the recording changes the time map; keep the old version rather than silently reusing stale links. Asset identity must survive storage moves but change when the underlying cut changes.

Separate modalities in candidate generation

Transcript search works for spoken terms; frame descriptions or image embeddings may find a visual action with no spoken mention. Run each path within a budget, then combine candidates using calibrated ranks and overlap rules. A camera view of a valve does not prove that the narrator's pressure number belongs to that valve. Preserve which modality supplied each clue. Federated budgets prevent one long transcript from consuming every result slot.

Account for timing errors

Automatic speech recognition can mishear part numbers, names and negation. Speaker diarization can swap labels after cross-talk. Store word-level confidence or review status where available, and include a small playback margin around candidate spans. Avoid letting margins turn a thirty-second citation into an unrelated ten-minute clip. When the spoken answer is uncertain, retrieve nearby segments or abstain rather than silently repairing the transcript. Abstention should remain available after a high ranking score.

Check the answer at playback time

A timestamp is a pointer, not proof. The final claim should be checked against the media span and any displayed text within it. For a question about who approved a release, both speaker attribution and the words of approval matter. If the text says 'not approved', a frame showing a green button cannot reverse it. Keep transcript and frame citations separate when both are needed. Support checks must inspect the exact moment behind each claim.

Evaluate with time tolerance

Judge answer-bearing intervals, not just media IDs. Measure whether the right asset entered the candidate set, whether an overlapping interval appeared in the top window, and whether the final answer cited a span narrow enough to inspect. Include edits, repeated phrases, noisy speech, overlapping speakers and purely visual evidence. Report timing error and missing-evidence abstention separately. A result that finds the correct meeting but points nine minutes late should fail the timestamp test.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class MediaSegment:
    asset_id: str
    version: str
    start_ms: int
    end_ms: int
    speaker: str
    transcript: str

def timed_matches(segments: list[MediaSegment], asset_id: str,
                  version: str, phrase: str) -> list[tuple[int, int, str]]:
    matches = []
    for segment in segments:
        if segment.start_ms < 0 or segment.end_ms <= segment.start_ms:
            raise ValueError("invalid media interval")
        if segment.asset_id == asset_id and segment.version == version \
                and phrase.casefold() in segment.transcript.casefold():
            matches.append((segment.start_ms, segment.end_ms, segment.speaker))
    return matches

meeting = [MediaSegment("release-briefing", "cut-3", 83000, 97000,
                        "release-lead", "The patch remains blocked."),
           MediaSegment("release-briefing", "cut-2", 79000, 93000,
                        "release-lead", "The patch is approved.")]
assert timed_matches(meeting, "release-briefing", "cut-3", "blocked") == [
    (83000, 97000, "release-lead")]
assert timed_matches(meeting, "release-briefing", "cut-3", "approved") == []

Performance and operating cost

The baseline scans S segments in O(S) time and stores O(K) matches. A transcript term index narrows spoken candidates; visual embeddings add frame-sampling, index storage and ranking costs. Higher sampling density improves access to brief events but increases storage and search work. Evaluate timestamp recall against that cost, rather than indexing every frame by default.

Common Mistakes

  • Returning a meeting title without a timecoded supporting span.
  • Mixing transcript timestamps from one cut with video from another.
  • Treating noisy automatic captions as verified words.
  • Using a visual match to assert a speaker's words without checking the audio.

Validation drill

Judge 39 questions over six edited recordings. Include repeated phrases, overlapping speakers and silent visual events; measure asset recall, interval overlap, speaker accuracy and cited-span width.

title: Hard-negative mining without training against true answers
summary: Choose informative retrieval distractors while auditing labels, lineage and split leakage before model training.
body:
Choose informative retrieval distractors while auditing labels, lineage and split leakage before model training.

Define the negative precisely

A hard negative is a passage that resembles a relevant answer but does not satisfy the query. For a request for pump P-47's current relief limit, an old revision or P-48's limit may be informative distractors. A second valid P-47 passage is a false negative even if the judgment file omitted it. Before mining, specify query intent, time boundary, tenant and what counts as support. Judgment labels should allow multiple positives and an uncertain state; a missing label is not proof of irrelevance.

Mine from several candidate pools

Lexical search yields near-word matches; dense retrieval yields semantic neighbors; a reranker can find subtle confusions. Sample within authorized, training-eligible corpora and record which model and index version produced each candidate. Balance easy and hard distractors so training does not only distinguish almost-identical policies. A candidate that is too hard may actually be another answer, especially when multiple documents repeat the same fact. Lineage checks help distinguish a copied positive from a real contradiction.

Audit false negatives before training

Compare each mined candidate with all known positives by document lineage, answer entity, valid interval and evidence span. Flag near-identical answers and ambiguous cases for human review. Do not automatically turn every high-scoring unlabeled passage into a negative. If the corpus has a corrected revision, the old passage may be a legitimate negative for a current-policy query but a positive for an as-of query. Temporal eligibility belongs in the label, not only the search filter.

Prevent split leakage

A test question and a training question can differ in wording while pointing to the same source paragraph. Split by source lineage or entity family when the evaluation asks for transfer to unseen material. Keep mined examples from a fixed training snapshot; a later corpus refresh must not add evaluation positives to the training pool. Log query ID, passage ID, source revision, mine score, decision and reviewer. Release gates should compare held-out supported recall, not training loss alone.

Measure the cost of hardness

Run an ablation with the same query set and candidate budget: baseline negatives, reviewed hard negatives, and mixed difficulty. Track false-negative audit rate, candidate recall, top-k judged relevance and answer support on held-out slices. If mining improves ranking for common queries but harms a rare language or recent-policy slice, do not ship the aggregate gain as universal. Keep a small manual audit of top-ranked new negatives after each mining cycle; retriever changes alter which mistakes are selected next.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class MinedPassage:
    passage_id: str
    tenant: str
    lineage: str
    entity_id: str
    label: str
    score: float

def reviewed_negatives(candidates: list[MinedPassage], tenant: str,
                       positive_lineages: set[str], entity_id: str) -> list[str]:
    selected = [candidate for candidate in candidates
                if candidate.tenant == tenant and candidate.label == "negative"
                and candidate.lineage not in positive_lineages
                and candidate.entity_id != entity_id]
    return [candidate.passage_id for candidate in
            sorted(selected, key=lambda item: item.score, reverse=True)]

pool = [MinedPassage("pump-48", "plant-a", "manual-48", "pump-p48", "negative", .94),
        MinedPassage("copied-p47", "plant-a", "manual-47", "pump-p47", "negative", .99),
        MinedPassage("unreviewed", "plant-a", "manual-52", "pump-p52", "unknown", .96),
        MinedPassage("private", "plant-b", "manual-49", "pump-p49", "negative", .98)]
assert reviewed_negatives(pool, "plant-a", {"manual-47"}, "pump-p47") == ["pump-48"]

Performance and operating cost

Filtering N mined candidates costs O(N log N) time because the sample sorts by score, with O(N) extra space; a bounded top-k heap can reduce sorting work when N is large. The expensive part is creating and auditing labels: retrieval calls, cross-source comparisons and human adjudication. Spend that budget on candidates likely to change a decision, not on repeated copies of the same mistake.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating every unlabeled retrieved passage as a negative.
  • Mining a copied positive into the negative pool because it has a new URL.
  • Letting test-source lineages enter the training candidate pool.
  • Judging the mining run only by training loss or one aggregate retrieval score.

Validation drill

Mine 79 candidates for 23 queries from lexical and dense pools. Review ambiguous matches, split by document lineage, and compare held-out top-five relevance and supported-answer rate before accepting the new negatives.

  • Near-duplicate retrieval: collapse copies without hiding independent evidence
  • Temporal retrieval: answer as-of questions from valid evidence
  • Retrieval release gates: evaluate slices before changing an index

title: Query expansion: add recall terms without changing the user's question
summary: Use controlled synonyms and subqueries while retaining exact IDs, exclusions, dates and authorization scope.
body:
Use controlled synonyms and subqueries while retaining exact IDs, exclusions, dates and authorization scope.

Split immutable constraints from optional terms

Parse exact identifiers, quoted phrases, exclusions, tenant scope and time bounds before expansion. Keep those constraints attached to every generated subquery. A query for case AX-47 after September must not turn into a general query about delayed cases. Expansion is useful for vocabulary mismatch: ‘chargeback’ may appear as ‘payment dispute’ in a permitted document. It is not permission to relax an exact case ID. Routing should decide whether expansion is needed at all.

Bound candidates and weights

Start with a small, reviewed synonym list or a validated reformulator. Search the original query as one leg and each expansion as a separate leg, then merge by passage ID. Preserve which leg found each candidate. Weight the original query and exact-match leg so a broad synonym cannot bury the literal target. Rank fusion is a useful merge baseline because score scales from different legs are not directly comparable.

Reject drift

A proposed rewrite fails when it drops an identifier, changes a number, reverses a negation, broadens a tenant, or shifts a date interval. Compare parsed constraints before executing the rewrite. Some vocabulary changes are context dependent: ‘hold’ can mean a payment hold or warehouse hold. For ambiguous terms, retrieve with both senses only inside the authorized corpus and let evidence disambiguate; otherwise ask the user.

Measure value by query family

Expansion should improve recall for jargon and paraphrase queries without harming exact-ID precision or latency. Build paired judgments with original-only and expanded runs. Report newly found answer passages, false positives, average additional calls and p95 latency. Retain a no-answer set; a system that answers more questions by matching unrelated synonyms has not improved. Traces should expose which expansion introduced each candidate.

Worked contract

import re

def safe_expansions(question: str, synonyms: dict[str, tuple[str, ...]]) -> list[str]:
    required_ids = set(re.findall(r"\bAX-\d+\b", question.upper()))
    variants = [question]
    for term, replacements in synonyms.items():
        if not re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(term)}\b", question, re.IGNORECASE):
            continue
        for replacement in replacements[:2]:
            candidate = re.sub(rf"\b{re.escape(term)}\b", replacement,
                               question, count=1, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
            if required_ids <= set(re.findall(r"\bAX-\d+\b", candidate.upper())):
                variants.append(candidate)
    return variants[:4]

variants = safe_expansions("AX-47 chargeback status",
                           {"chargeback": ("payment dispute", "card dispute")})
assert variants == ["AX-47 chargeback status",
                    "AX-47 payment dispute status", "AX-47 card dispute status"]
assert all("AX-47" in variant for variant in variants)

Performance and operating cost

For Q query characters and at most S reviewed replacements, this small implementation scans O(SQ) time and stores at most four variants. Search cost can grow roughly with the number of variants, so cap expansion count and parallel calls. This demonstration protects exact IDs only; production validation must also compare negations, dates, tenant scope and other parsed constraints before dispatch.

Common Mistakes

  • Replacing an exact identifier with a likely-looking related identifier.
  • Dropping ‘not’ or a date bound while rewriting.
  • Merging scores from different search legs as if their scales were equal.
  • Celebrating recall gains without measuring no-answer false positives.

Validation drill

Judge 61 requests across exact IDs, jargon synonyms, negations, date bounds and no-answer cases. Compare original-only search with a maximum of three expanded variants; reject any rewrite that changes parsed constraints.

title: Knowledge graph retrieval: prove every edge in the path
summary: Use entity links to find candidate evidence while retaining the passage, relation type, revision and access rule that made each edge valid.
body:
Use entity links to find candidate evidence while retaining the passage, relation type, revision and access rule that made each edge valid.

Define the graph's evidence contract

Graph retrieval stores entities and typed relations so a question can follow connections that text similarity misses. Consider a service case linked to a replacement part, which is linked to a supplier bulletin. A bare edge saying that a case uses a part is insufficient: the edge also needs the source passage, relation type, effective time, extraction method and tenant. The graph is a navigation index, not an authority separate from its documents. Passage provenance lets a reviewer inspect the statement behind each edge.

Resolve entities before traversal

An identifier can be reused across tenants, and two supplier names can refer to one organization. Resolve an entity only within its namespace and permitted source set. Keep aliases as attributed claims rather than overwriting the canonical node. For an ambiguous name, return candidate entities with their disambiguating attributes; do not silently merge them. A false merge makes every later traversal look plausible. Exact identifiers should remain exact even when a semantic retriever proposes a near match.

Bound traversal and evidence assembly

Start from an authorized seed, expand only allowed relation types, cap hop count and degree, and reject a route if any edge lacks an active supporting passage. A popular supplier node may have thousands of neighbors; unrestricted breadth-first traversal can dominate latency and swamp the answer with irrelevant paths. Score the path by the weakest required edge and the question's relation sequence. Multi-hop stop rules should halt when the requested join is proven or the search budget expires.

Treat updates as graph operations

A document deletion must remove or invalidate all edges supported solely by that revision. If another active passage also supports an edge, the edge may survive with that other provenance. Keep an edge-to-passage reverse map to make revocation prompt. During a rebuild, compare node and edge counts by tenant, then test a set of known paths and forbidden paths before swapping the graph generation. Versioned ingestion prevents an old event from reviving a revoked relation.

Judge paths, not fluent answers

Create questions with known seed nodes, expected relation sequences and expected supporting passages. Report seed resolution, edge recall, valid-path recall and final claim support separately. Include a shared-name trap, a stale edge, a missing middle relation, a high-degree hub and a cross-tenant decoy. If the result uses a correct answer reached through unsupported edges, mark the path wrong: the route will fail on the next corpus revision.

Worked contract

from collections import deque
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SupportedEdge:
    source: str
    target: str
    relation: str
    tenant: str
    passage_id: str

def evidence_paths(edges: list[SupportedEdge], start: str, goal: str,
                   tenant: str, allowed: tuple[str, ...], degree_cap: int = 24):
    adjacency: dict[str, list[SupportedEdge]] = {}
    for edge in edges:
        if edge.tenant == tenant and edge.passage_id:
            adjacency.setdefault(edge.source, []).append(edge)
    frontier = deque([(start, ())])
    while frontier:
        node, path = frontier.popleft()
        if len(path) == len(allowed):
            if node == goal:
                return path
            continue
        candidates = [edge for edge in adjacency.get(node, ())
                      if edge.relation == allowed[len(path)]]
        for edge in candidates[:degree_cap]:
            if edge.target not in {start, *(part.target for part in path)}:
                frontier.append((edge.target, path + (edge,)))
    return ()

links = [SupportedEdge("case-47", "part-83", "uses", "north", "case-r2"),
         SupportedEdge("part-83", "bulletin-29", "covered-by", "north", "notice-r4"),
         SupportedEdge("part-83", "bulletin-91", "covered-by", "south", "private-r3")]
path = evidence_paths(links, "case-47", "bulletin-29", "north",
                      ("uses", "covered-by"))
assert [edge.passage_id for edge in path] == ["case-r2", "notice-r4"]
assert evidence_paths(links, "case-47", "bulletin-91", "north",
                      ("uses", "covered-by")) == ()

Performance and operating cost

Building the in-memory adjacency map costs O(E) time and space for E eligible edges. A bounded traversal can still examine up to the degree cap raised to the hop count; keep both limits small and index relation plus tenant in persistent storage. The example returns the first valid path, not the globally best path, and production ranking needs judged evidence quality.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating an extracted relation as fact after its supporting passage was deleted.
  • Merging two tenants' same-named entities into one node.
  • Allowing a high-degree node to expand without a cap.
  • Citing only the final bulletin when the answer depends on two edges.

Validation drill

Construct 43 questions against a small case-part-bulletin graph. Remove six supporting passages and verify that the affected paths disappear, while paths with independent support remain.

title: Multimodal retrieval: connect images, OCR and text to one asset identity
summary: Search image-bearing documents while keeping captions, OCR text, crop coordinates and permissions tied to the exact source revision.
body:
Search image-bearing documents while keeping captions, OCR text, crop coordinates and permissions tied to the exact source revision.

Define the asset graph

A diagram may have a text caption, OCR labels, a surrounding paragraph and a visual embedding. Give all views one immutable asset revision, then store their own modality and location. A match in OCR is evidence for visible words, not for a visual relation that OCR cannot read. A visual similarity match locates candidate images; it does not prove that two valves have the same operating limit. Source provenance must survive the modality change.

Retrieve and fuse carefully

Text queries can search captions and OCR; image queries can use visual embeddings. Fuse candidate asset IDs only after permission and revision checks. Preserve the match route in the result: caption, OCR, surrounding text or image similarity. This matters when a reviewer asks why a drawing ranked first. Rerank with the full question and a bounded set of candidate assets, not a collection of detached crop embeddings.

Resolve the cited region

An answer about a label in the upper-left crop should cite that region and its parent page. Store normalized crop coordinates and the original image dimensions so a viewer can highlight the right area. If preprocessing rotates or resizes the image, transform coordinates back before presenting them. A citation to an entire manual page may be too broad when the claim depends on a tiny annotation. Support checks should confirm the cited modality can prove the claim.

Measure modality-specific misses

Maintain query slices for exact OCR strings, paraphrased captions, visual resemblance and questions requiring both text and image. Evaluate candidate recall by modality and asset revision. A high combined score can conceal that OCR systematically misses rotated labels. Keep a no-answer slice where a visually similar image lacks the requested label, and require the system to say so.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AssetView:
    asset_id: str
    revision: str
    tenant: str
    modality: str
    content: str

def find_label(views: list[AssetView], label: str, tenant: str,
               active_revisions: dict[str, str]) -> list[str]:
    return sorted({view.asset_id for view in views
                   if view.tenant == tenant and view.modality == "ocr"
                   and active_revisions.get(view.asset_id) == view.revision
                   and label.casefold() in view.content.casefold()})

views = [AssetView("pump-47", "r3", "plant-a", "ocr", "Outlet 47 kPa"),
         AssetView("pump-47", "r2", "plant-a", "ocr", "Outlet 73 kPa"),
         AssetView("pump-47", "r3", "plant-b", "ocr", "Outlet 47 kPa")]
assert find_label(views, "47 kPa", "plant-a", {"pump-47": "r3"}) == ["pump-47"]
assert find_label(views, "73 kPa", "plant-a", {"pump-47": "r3"}) == []

Performance and operating cost

The sample scans V views in O(V) time and uses O(A) result space for A matching assets. Production retrieval can index each modality, but storage and embedding work grow with the number of views and crops. Set crop limits and deduplicate near-identical renders; otherwise one document can flood the candidate window.

Common Mistakes

  • Using visual similarity as proof of a printed numeric label.
  • Returning a crop without its parent asset and revision.
  • Mixing a fresh caption with OCR from an old image revision.
  • Showing a broad page citation when only one crop supports the answer.

Validation drill

Index 17 diagrams with captions and OCR, including three rotated scans and two superseded revisions. Judge exact-label, visual and mixed queries separately; verify every cited crop opens at the correct page and coordinates.

title: Retrieval evaluation labels: build a trustworthy judged set
summary: Create passage-level judgments with time, permission and disagreement rules so release scores mean the same thing across runs.
body:
Create passage-level judgments with time, permission and disagreement rules so release scores mean the same thing across runs.

Define the unit of judgment

A retrieval test needs a question, corpus snapshot, principal scope, answerable state and one or more supporting passage IDs. Labeling only a final answer string loses the evidence path: two passages may express the same value, but only one may be active for the query date or visible to the principal. Include the exact fact or relation each passage supports. Claim-level support can then be checked without treating a merely related document as a positive hit.

Collect questions from distinct failures

Sample real query shapes only where consent and access rules allow it. Add exact-ID requests, paraphrases, two-hop joins, table calculations, time-bounded questions, revoked documents, ambiguous names and no-answer cases. Synthetic queries are useful for rare traps, but they should be reviewed against an actual corpus snapshot. Keep a held-out set that prompt and ranker tuning cannot see. Otherwise the next release may memorize the test's wording instead of improving retrieval.

Make disagreement visible

Two reviewers should independently judge a difficult slice. If one marks a passage relevant because it mentions the same topic while the other requires the answer-bearing sentence, the rubric is incomplete. Record both labels and a resolution reason; do not silently average them. A third reviewer can adjudicate disputed examples. Store the rubric version with each label, because changing 'relevant' from topical to supporting changes every reported metric.

Lock the evaluation context

A query that was answerable on Monday may be unanswerable after a Tuesday deletion. Freeze or identify the corpus generation, permission policy and query-as-of time for each run. When the source changes, create a new judgment revision instead of overwriting the old one. Generation swaps and access rules are part of the test context, not incidental metadata.

Report slices with uncertainty

Measure recall at the candidate window, recall after reranking, citation support and abstention accuracy by question family. A single mean hides a catastrophic permission regression in a small slice. For a tiny slice, show counts along with percentages rather than implying precision the data cannot support. Attach first-loss traces for every regression; that makes adjudication and repair practical instead of a debate over one aggregate score.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Judgment:
    question_id: str
    corpus_generation: str
    visible_passages: frozenset[str]
    supporting_passages: frozenset[str]
    candidate_passages: tuple[str, ...]

def recall_at_window(judgments: list[Judgment]) -> tuple[int, int]:
    found = eligible = 0
    for judgment in judgments:
        gold = judgment.supporting_passages & judgment.visible_passages
        if not gold:
            continue
        eligible += 1
        found += bool(gold & set(judgment.candidate_passages))
    return found, eligible

cases = [Judgment("q-47", "g-8", frozenset({"policy-r3"}),
                  frozenset({"policy-r3"}), ("policy-r3", "memo-r2")),
         Judgment("q-48", "g-8", frozenset({"memo-r2"}),
                  frozenset({"private-r7"}), ("private-r7",)),
         Judgment("q-49", "g-8", frozenset({"manual-r4"}),
                  frozenset({"manual-r4"}), ("notice-r1",))]
assert recall_at_window(cases) == (1, 2)

Performance and operating cost

This simple metric scans each candidate list once, O(C) time for C total candidates, and builds temporary sets up to the window size. Human labeling and adjudication dominate cost. The example excludes questions with no eligible supporting passage; report those separately as no-answer and permission slices rather than burying them in recall.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating a topical passage as if it supported the requested fact.
  • Changing the corpus or permission scope while comparing two releases.
  • Discarding reviewer disagreement instead of fixing the rubric.
  • Reporting only a pooled metric that conceals no-answer or restricted-document failures.

Validation drill

Label 72 questions in six families, including 12 no-answer cases. Double-label 18 difficult examples and adjudicate disagreements before comparing two retrieval releases on the same corpus generation.
